title: THE NEW FOREST
description: Royal hunting forest created in 1079 by the enlargement of Saxon hunting grounds and woodland. This involved the moving of some settlements which were situated on the edge of the original hunting area. The bounds of the forest created in 1079 were expanded during the 12th century but were reinstated following the Magna Carter in 1215 and the Charter of the New Forest in 1217. These bounds were again revoked in 1227 but back in place from 1300 until 1327 when replaced by bounds implemented by the Charter of the New Forest which remained in place until the New Forest Act of 1964. The forest was used for coppicing, first documented in 1389. Oak was used for shipbuilding, mainly during the 16th century.

title: NEW FOREST UNION WORKHOUSE
description: The workhouse was built in the 1830s and stylistically appears to have been designed by Sampsom Kempthorne. The site consists of a two and three storey Y-shaped bblock within an octagon defined by single storey buildings and the single storey administrative range on the west. The church to the north of the workhouse is a later addition. The buildings are of red brick, now painted, with slate roofs. The north half of the workhouse was occupied by women and the south half by men. The workhouse is now in use as a hospital.

title: Middle Field Farm- New Forest
description: A detailed gradiometry survey was conducted over approximately 28.2 hectares of agricultural  land. A small number of anomalies of a probable and possible archaeological origin have been  identified within the survey area including linear and curvi-linear anomalies throughout the  site. These indicate the presence of cut features and banks of an archaeological origin and  may be related to former field boundaries or trackways that appear on historic mapping of the  site. There are also areas of magnetic variation in the west of the site which may be of an  archaeological origin related to the plantation; however their ambiguous shape means that  they could also have been caused by natural pedology.  In the centre and south west of the site there are areas of modern agricultural activity such as  ploughing, and there are a number of modern services present in the eastern half of the  survey area. There are areas of land drains in the north and east of the site and areas of  magnetic disturbance, scattered magnetic debris and a collection of magnetic spikes probably  caused by modern ferrous rubbish are also present in throughout the survey area. A small  area of natural geological variation is also present to the north.
creator: Orlando Prestidge

title: Buckler's Hard, Beaulieu, New Forest, Hampshire
description: Wessex Archaeology was commissioned by the New Forest National Park Authority (NFNPA) to undertake an archaeological excavation adjacent to the riverfront at Buckler's Hard, Beaulieu, Hampshire (NGR 441000 100100). This evaluation formed part of the Festival of British Archaeology 2012 as well as being part of the New Forest National Park New Forest Remembers - Untold Stories of World War II project. It was also hoped that the project could act as an evaluation for a proposed replica shipwright's workshop.  In addition to the initial three trenches outlined in the Written Scheme of Investigation, two further test pits and five other excavation areas were opened up in order to target better the proposed building footprint and to assess and investigate the concrete slipway.  In the area to the west of the slipway the evaluation was able to demonstrate that substantial levelling and landscaping had taken place after the war and the majority of the structures have been comprehensively demolished.
creator: Naomi Brennan

title: New Forest, South East Mixed (Wooded)
description: This is an elevated plateau that lies between the Avon Valley (to the west) and the Test Valley and Southampton Water (to the east). Its southern boundary is bounded by the Solent and its northern boundary extends into Wiltshire. The area is a mosaic of ancient woodland, wood pasture, heath, grassland, pasture and arable farmland. Of the area, 29% is in agricultural use and 31% is woodland. There is a surprising amount of built development, particularly around the edges of the area: 9.5% is urban. The remainder of the Character Area is defined as upland, semi-natural or coastal land. The majority (85.9%) is in the New Forest National Park.

title: Bilcombes Field, Fawley, New Forest: Archaeological Evaluation
description: The evaluation fieldwork comprised the excavation of 20 trenches, each measuring 30m x 1.8m. The trenches were located to provide a 5% representative sample of the remainder of the site. Two trenches have been placed to target linear features of possible archaeological origin identified from cropmark evidence as part of the NMP. The remaining trenches have been located to target areas of proposed impact, which are the footprints of the proposed haul road and the proposed site compound and the location of proposed drains and soakaway pits. In February and March 2023 Cotswold Archaeology carried out an archaeological evaluation at Bilcombes Field, Fawley, New Forest. A total of twenty trenches were excavated, with six trenches containing archaeological features. Of the six trenches containing archaeological features, four of the trenches contained ditches containing no datable material but which are likely to be medieval/post-medieval field boundaries associated with the cropmarks identified on the Historic England National Mapping Programme. Four pits were also recorded with one containing post-medieval brick fragments.
